accuracy.evidence: Matches the three evidence statements of the topic: attentive listening (the four-part listening body: look, quiet mouth, still hands, face the speaker), following discussion rules (waiting for the speaker to finish, passing a talking object to a raised hand, hand up and wait to be asked) and showing understanding by responding (picture that matches every word of a request, a reply that fits a friend's news). Wording follows the English national curriculum spoken-language aim 'listen and respond appropriately to adults and their peers' and the EYFS early learning goal for listening, attention and understanding. Eye contact is presented as 'look at them', not as a strict rule.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets what 4-6 year olds actually get wrong in group talk: calling out or talking over the speaker (turn step blocks the pass while the bubble still says 'Still talking', challenge 'over'/'call'), replying about yourself instead of the friend's news ('I like cake', 'Look at me!', challenge 'off'), catching only the key noun and missing a colour, number or position word (red/blue cup, on/under the bed, one/two balls, challenge 'miss'), fidgeting with a toy while listening ('toy'), and nodding or guessing instead of asking for a repeat ('guess', m4).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics are specific to turn-taking talk: a talking ball that can only move after a timed speech bubble finishes and only to a raised hand; a listener whose four behaviours each reveal more of the speaker's words; drawn picture choices that differ by one function word; a reply chooser judged on relevance; and a hand-up-then-wait sequence with a teacher who calls on you after a pause. None of these could be relabelled for another topic, and the 6-token shingle gate passed against every flagship lab, including flagqw, flagprint and flagmood.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers each rule by doing: passing early is refused with 'Wait! Mia is still talking'; Gran's sentence is literally greyed out and gappy until Pip looks, is quiet, keeps still and faces her, so listening behaviour visibly changes what is heard; the picture step shows that one small word (red, under, two, big) changes the right answer; and in the hand-up step the answer button only works after the teacher says 'Yes, Pip?'. The text after each task names the rule the child just used.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions each have a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: 'Mia is talking. When can Leo talk? Now, any time' (the pass is refused until she finishes), 'Pip plays with a car and looks away. Will Pip hear all Gran says? Yes' (the words stay hidden until all four parts are fixed), and 'Ava says I got a puppy, Leo says I like cake. Did Leo listen? Yes' (the cake reply is marked as off-topic).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge kinds (wait, show, fits, hand, word, again) rotate with shuffled answer order, and each wrong answer gets its own message naming the slip: 'If two talk at once, nobody hears', 'A toy pulls your eyes and ears away', 'Trains are not about the dog. Answer what Leo said', 'Laughing at sad news hurts', 'Shouting out takes a turn from others', 'Gran said blue. Listen to every word' and 'Guessing can go wrong. It is fine to ask again'. Wrong taps inside the lab steps also get specific feedback (e.g. 'That cup is blue. Gran said red').

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs score FK 0.2 (family limit 5.0) with short sentences and everyday words (look, quiet, still, wait, fits); adult text scores FK 6.8. In the lab every instruction is one short line, pictures carry the meaning in the matching step so a pre-reader can play with a grown-up reading the bubble, and the lab uses the young class (56 px buttons, larger step text).

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph does one job (how to look like a listener, wait for the end, every word matters, reply so it fits or ask again). Adult paragraphs cover the curriculum link, how the lab makes waiting visible, named common mistakes, and a dinner-table talking-spoon routine. Each of the six lab steps practises a different part of the skill and none repeats another.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 (390 px) screenshots in dark and light themes for every step before and after Show me. The four children, speech bubble and ball fit the rug view; behaviour boxes were shortened after the first check clipped 'Look out of the window' (now 'Looks away'); the three picture tiles are about 110 px wide; reply bubbles span the width at about 55 px tall; every canvas action also has a 56 px button below.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: 'Ball to Leo/Ava/Pip', the four listening behaviours, 'Picture 1-3' with aria-labels describing each picture ('red cup', 'cat under the bed', 'two big balls'), each reply, and 'Hand up' / 'Say ...'. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action with who is talking, what they said and what to do next. The challenge uses a polite live region, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) was clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
